segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But as for you, speak what befits healthy teaching.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Older men are to be sober, dignified, self-controlled, healthy in faith, in love, in endurance.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Older women likewise are to bear themselves as befits what is sacred: not slanderers, not enslaved to much wine, but teachers of what is good,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that they may school the young women in self-control, to love their husbands, to love their children,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to be self-controlled, pure, workers at home, good, subject to their own husbands, so that the word of God may not be reviled.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Urge the younger men likewise to be self-controlled.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In every respect present yourself as a model of good works, showing in your teaching integrity, dignity,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and healthy speech that is beyond reproach, so that the opponent may be put to shame, having nothing bad to say about us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Slaves are to be subject to their own masters in everything, to be pleasing, not talking back,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: not pilfering, but showing all good faithfulness, so that in everything they may adorn the teaching of God our Saviour.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all people,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: training us so that, renouncing irreverence and worldly desires, we might live with self-control, justly, and reverently in the present age,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: awaiting the blessed hope and appearing of the glory of our great God and Saviour, Jesus Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people of his very own, zealous for good works.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Speak these things; urge and rebuke with all authority. Let no one look down on you.

notes.note: The Greek word is the ordinary one for being in good health, and the letters to Timothy and Titus use it against teaching pictured as diseased. 'Sound' is the traditional rendering and is not wrong, but the medical image has faded from it. The same word recurs in verse 2 ('healthy in faith') and verse 8 ('healthy speech'), and is rendered the same way each time.

This word names one of the classic Greek virtues: a steady, well-governed mind that keeps impulses in check. Its word-family runs through the chapter (verses 2, 4, 5, 6 and 12), asked in turn of older men, young women, younger men and all believers. English versions usually vary the rendering; here it is kept as 'self-control' throughout so the repetition can be heard. The verb in verse 4, usually translated 'train' or 'encourage', is from the same family, hence 'school in self-control'.

The word describes what is fitting for sacred persons, places or rites, and was used of priestly conduct and religious ceremony. The traditional 'reverent' is weaker and suggests an inner attitude, where the Greek speaks of outward bearing suited to holy service. The rendering also keeps the link with 'befits' in verse 1.

The earliest manuscripts have a rare word meaning 'working at home'. Many later manuscripts have a common word differing by one letter, meaning 'staying at home' or 'keeping house', which lies behind the older English rendering. The following word, 'good', can also be read with this one ('good household managers'). Most editors and translations treat it as a separate item, as here, sometimes rendering it 'kind'.

This verb and the noun 'appearing' in verse 13 belong together. In the period they were used for a god's visible intervention to help and for the public arrival of a ruler, and 'saviour' was likewise a title given to gods and kings. The passage frames Christ's first coming and his awaited return as two such appearances.

notes.traditional: that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men
notes.note: 'To all people' can attach either to 'bringing salvation' or to 'has appeared'. Most modern translations take the first, as here: the grace is saving for everyone. Some older versions take the second: the grace that saves has appeared to everyone.

The Greek sets a noun and an adverb from one word-family against each other: what is renounced and how one is then to live. The family denotes proper reverence toward the divine, shown in conduct, and its absence. The traditional 'ungodliness' and 'godly' keep the pairing but are vague in modern English; 'irreverence' and 'reverently' keep it and are closer to how the words were used.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice. The adverb here describes conduct that is right, especially toward other people, and 'justly' is the natural English for that. The related noun is rendered 'righteousness' in this translation, as in most English versions.

notes.phrase: our great God and Saviour, Jesus Christ
notes.traditional: the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ
notes.note: In the Greek a single article governs 'God' and 'Saviour', which most grammarians and most modern translations take to mean one person: Jesus Christ is called 'our great God and Saviour'. The older rendering distinguishes two, God and Christ, and a minority take 'Jesus Christ' as explaining 'the glory' of God. 'Appearing of the glory' can also be read as 'glorious appearing'.

notes.phrase: a people of his very own
notes.note: This rare word comes from the Greek Old Testament, where it describes Israel as God's treasured possession at Sinai (Exodus 19:5; Deuteronomy 7:6; 14:2). The verse as a whole echoes Scripture's language of God redeeming Israel from its lawless deeds and cleansing a people for himself (Psalm 130:8; Ezekiel 37:23). The older 'peculiar' meant 'belonging specially to one owner', a sense the word has lost.

candidates.reason: The σωφρον- family (adjective, verb, adverb, noun) recurs across the Pastorals, Paul, Mark, Luke, Acts and 1 Peter, and versions scatter it across 'sober', 'sensible', 'prudent', 'self-controlled' and 'in one's right mind'; it also needs distinguishing from ἐγκράτεια.
'Sound doctrine' versus 'healthy teaching' needs one decision for the Pastorals, where the medical metaphor is deliberate and repeated, and for literal uses in Luke and 3 John.

The εὐσεβ-/ἀσεβ- family ('godliness', 'piety', 'devotion', 'reverence', and 'ungodly') is frequent in the Pastorals, 2 Peter, Acts, Romans and Jude and needs one paired rendering so the positive and negative terms stay visibly related.

Used of wives, slaves, citizens, church members and Christ across many books; 'submit', 'be subject', 'be subordinate' and 'obey' carry different connotations and should not vary by context without a decision.

'Slave', 'servant' and 'bondservant' compete across the whole New Testament, both for literal slaves and as a self-description of apostles, and inconsistency would mislead readers about the social reality.
